Static safety architectures fail because developers cannot whiteboard emergent risks. Modern software engineering proves this. Stripe shipped their MVP in 60 days and refactored based on live production data. That live data caught drift that pre-deployment checks completely missed. We must judge AI systems by court-admissible runtime telemetry, not by the thickness of their compliance binders. When Congress defines a defect by missing paperwork rather than missing telemetry, you hand market control to legacy monopolies. They alone can afford the 18-month compliance delay.

Safety advocates demand standardized documentation because they believe raw telemetry is legally unaccountable. I accept that premise for legacy IT systems. But applying that standard to AI deployment carries a lethal opportunity cost. The FDA historically took 12 years to approve standard medical devices under static safety frameworks. If regulators freeze AI medical deployment to wait for bureaucratic monitoring approvals, we explicitly choose to let patients die. We could automate cures for those diseases today. The cost of this delay falls on the sick. The beneficiaries are incumbent tech giants building regulatory moats. We need automated, cascaded activation monitoring that triggers on actual system drift. We do not need aviation-style reporting that just causes alert fatigue.

The precise threshold for a legal design defect must be the absence of automated telemetry in high-stakes, cyber-physical deployments. When an autonomous grid controller lacks real-time drift monitoring and causes a $50 million operational shutdown, that is a defect. The enforcement mechanism is strict liability for unmonitored physical damage. Existing tort law handles this perfectly. We do not need new pre-deployment gatekeepers. This approach is politically feasible because it aligns consumer protection with permissionless innovation. It mirrors the 1996 Telecommunications Act. That legislation shielded platforms from intermediary liability while punishing direct harm. Expanding "design defect" to include low-stakes software lacking documented frameworks outlaws open-source development. You trade human flourishing for institutional paralysis.
